docs.title: Linear Regression
docs.text: Linear regression is one of the simplest and most widely used machine learning techniques. It models the relationship between an input variable (or several inputs) and an output variable by fitting a straight line (or hyperplane) through the data.

docs.title: The Equation
docs.text:
For a single input variable \( x \), the model is:

\[ y = w x + b \]
  • \( y \) → predicted output
  • \( x \) → input variable
  • \( w \) → weight (slope of the line)
  • \( b \) → bias (intercept)

For multiple input variables:

\[ y = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_n x_n + b \]

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Inputs: numerical data (e.g., beam length, load, temperature).
  • Outputs: a predicted continuous value (e.g., deflection, stress, efficiency).
  • Goal: find the best line (or hyperplane) that minimizes the difference between predicted and actual values.

docs.title: Engineering Applications
docs.text:
• Predicting material properties (e.g., tensile strength vs. composition).
  • Estimating drag coefficient from geometry.
  • Correlating beam deflection with load and length.

Note

Linear regression is often used as a baseline model. If it performs well, more complex machine learning models may not be needed.

docs.title: Machine Learning for Engineers, not data scientists
docs.text:
We believe Machine Learning has huge untapped potential in enginering problems, and believe the piece of the puzzle missing is that good ML models require domain knowledge, something only engineers can provide.

We aim for this site to become an open-source wiki page designed to minimise time to ML production for engineers to gain useful insights into complex systems.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Although the site functions as a library and can be read in any order, beginners are encouraged to follow the sections in sequence to build a complete foundation before starting their own projects.

Contributions to the wiki can be made through our GitHub repository . In the future, we plan to expand the site with a community forum and a blog for user-submitted projects and tutorials, however for now feel free to direct any questions on the Github discussion board.

docs.title: Books
docs.text:
• Approaching machine learning problems in computational fluid dynamics and computer aided engineering applications: A Monograph for Beginners - Dr Justin Hodges - A crash course in ML integration in engineering, easy to read.
  • Data-Driven Science and Engineering - J. Nathan Kutz and Steven L. Brunton - A deep dive into the maths used in scientific ML with lots of applied code
  • Hands on Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras, and TensorFlow - Aurelien Geron - Implementations for almost any ML model you might need

docs.title: About the creator
docs.text:
Joel Corbishley is an Aerospace Engineer with a Master’s degree from the University of Leeds, specialising in Computational Fluid Dynamics and Machine Learning in Engineering. He has hands-on experience in aerodynamic design, structural analysis and simulation development and has led multiple research and student projects in these areas.

The project grew out of a realisation that many engineers are curious about machine learning but are discouraged by the mathematical depth of most resources. Engineering ML Wiki focuses on a results-driven hands-on approach, emphasising real-world workflows, reproducible examples, and collaboration.

He is currently open to opportunities in software, simulation, or applied ML.
